OBJECTIVES:
By the end of this lecture students should be able to describe:

Superior Mediastinum

Inferior Mediastinum (Anterior, Middle, Posterior)

Clinical cases: 
Thoracic aortic aneurysm
Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

MEDIASTINUM

It is space on each side of 
the median plane between 
the two pleural sacs

It contains all the structures 
in the thorax, except the 
lungs and pleurae

Borders: it extends from 
the thoracic inlet to the 
diaphragm inferiorly and 
from the sternum and costal 
cartilages anteriorly to the 
bodies of the thoracic 
vertebrae posteriorly
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Divisions of mediastinum

Superior Mediastinum

extends from the thoracic inlet to 
the level of the sternal angle 
anteriorly and IV T4/5 posteriorly

Inferior Mediastinum

Anterior mediastinum: located 
between the sternum and 
pericardial sac

Middle mediastinum: located 
between the anterior and posterior 
mediastinum

Posterior mediastinum: located 
between the pericardial sac and 
thoracic vertebrae
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Superior mediastinum
Contents:

Anteriorly: thymus gland
(or its remains) and great 
veins 

In the middle: aortic arch
and its 3 great branches, 
vagus nerves, phrenic 
nerves

Posteriorly: trachea, 
esophagus, left recurrent 
laryngeal nerve, thoracic 
duct 
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Superior mediastinum

Improperly done 
sternal puncture 
may affect 
structures related 
to the posterior 
surface of the 
manubrium 
sternum:
1. In upper part –
Left 
brachiocephalic 
vein
2. In lower part –
Aortic arch

Inferior mediastinum:
Anterior mediastinum
Contents:  

Thymus gland

Lymph nodes

Fat
Thymus - lymphoid organ 

It is the site at which 
immature lymphocytes 
develop into T-
lymphocytes and secrete 
thymic hormones (they 
cause T lymphocytes to gain 
immunocompetence). 

It begins involution after 
puberty.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Middle mediastinum
Contents: 

Heart within the 
pericardium

Roots of the great vessels
(aorta, pulmonary arteries, 
and veins, SVC & IVC)

Phrenic nerves

Main bronchi

Arch of the azygos vein
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Posterior 
mediastinum
Contents:

Esophagus (#5) (with 
vagal plexuses)

Descending aorta
and branches

Azygos (#8) and 
Hemiazygos venous 
systems

Thoracic duct

Sympathetic trunk
(#21) and splanchnic 
nerves (#19)
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Superior vena cava (SVC)

It formed by the union of 
the right and left 
brachiocephalic veins –
roots of SVC

It contains all the venous 
blood from the head, neck, 
and upper limbs

It is joined by the azygos
vein (the one tributary) on 
its posterior aspect just 
before it pierces the 
pericardium
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Brachiocephalic veins

Right brachiocephalic 
vein – formed at the root of 
the neck by the union of the 
right subclavian and right 
internal jugular veins

Left brachiocephalic vein
– formed at the root of the 
neck by the union of the left 
subclavian and left internal 
jugular veins
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Azygos veinous system

It consists of the azygos
vein on the right side and 
the superior and inferior 
hemiazygos veins on the 
left which join the azygos 
vein

It drains blood from the 
posterior parts of 
intercostal spaces, 
posterior abdominal wall 
pericardium, diaphragm, 
bronchi, and esophagus
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Inferior vena cava (IVC)

It contains venous blood 
from the lower half of the 
body (GI organs, kidneys, 
reproductive viscera, lower 
limbs, etc.)

It pierces the central 
tendon of the diaphragm
at the level of T8
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pulmonary Veins

4 Pulmonary Veins - carry 
oxygenated blood back to 
the left atrium of the heart 
from the lungs.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Aorta

It is the main arterial trunk 
of the human body

It delivers oxygenated blood 
from the left ventricle to the 
body tissues

There are 3 parts:
Ascending aorta
Arch of the aorta
Descending aorta 
(diaphragm divided it on 
thoracic & abdominal -
level T12)
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Ascending aorta

It lies behind the 
sternum and becomes 
continuous with the 
aortic arch at the level 
of the sternal angle

branches: right and 
left coronary arteries
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Arch of the aorta

It begins as a continuation of the 
ascending aorta at the level of the 
sternal angle

It arches upward & backward to 
the left in front of the trachea, 
then down to the left of the 
trachea to become continuous with 
the descending aorta at the level 
of the sternal angle
Branches:

Brachiocephalic trunk – divides 
into the right common carotid and 
right subclavian arteries behind the 
right sternoclavicular joint

Left common carotid artery

Left subclavian artery
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Thoracic aortic aneurysm

Aneurysm of the aortic arch
compresses the left recurrent 
laryngeal nerve, leading to 
coughing, hoarseness, and 
paralysis of the ipsilateral vocal 
cord. It may cause dysphagia 
(difficulty in swallowing), resulting 
from pressure on the esophagus, 
and dyspnea (difficulty in 
breathing), resulting from pressure 
on the trachea, root of the lung, or 
phrenic nerve

Aneurysm of the thoracic aorta
may compress and tug on the 
trachea with each cardiac systole so 
that the aneurysm can be felt by 
palpating the trachea at the 
sternal notch (T2).
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Thoracic aorta
(thoracic portion of descending aorta)

It begins as a continuation of 
the arch of the aorta at the 
level of the sternal angle

runs downward in the 
posterior mediastinum
and pierces the diaphragm 
at the level of T12
Branches:

Posterior intercostal 
arteries & subcostal arteries

Superior phrenic arteries 

Pericardial, Esophageal 
and Bronchial arteries
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pulmonary trunk

conveys deoxygenated 
blood from the right 
ventricle to the lungs

terminates in the concavity 
of the aortic arch
Branches:

Right pulmonary artery

Left pulmonary artery
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Ligamentum arteriosum

It is a fibrous band that 
connects the bifurcation of 
the pulmonary trunk to the 
concavity of the aortic arch

It represents the remains of 
the ductus arteriosus 

Ductus arteriosus in the 
fetus conducts blood from 
the pulmonary trunk to the 
aorta, bypassing the lungs
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Patent ductus arteriosus 
(PDA)

It results from failure of the ductus 
arteriosus (a connection between the 
pulmonary trunk and aorta) to constrict 
and close after birth. 

Patients are present with a machine-like
diastolic and systolic murmur heard 
over the left sternoclavicular joint.

Prostaglandin E and low O2 tension 
sustain patency of the ductus arteriosus in 
the fetal period.

PDA is common in premature infants and in 
cases of maternal rubella infection. 

Left –to-right shunt increased pressure in 
pulmonary circulation (pulmonary 
hypertension) and is non-cyanotic

Treatment: surgical division and ligation
imperative. In great danger is left 
recurrent nerve (wrapping aorta arch). 
Injure of this nerve results in hoarseness. 
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

ESOPHAGUS

Muscular tube extending from the 
superior mediastinum through 
the posterior mediastinum that 
serves to convey food from the 
pharynx to the stomach

It starts at the level of the cricoid 
cartilage (C6), pierces the 
diaphragm at the level of T10, 
and descends another inch before 
it becomes continuous with the 
stomach

Muscular wall consists of skeletal 
muscle in its upper third, 
smooth muscle in its lower
third, and a combination of both 
in the middle third
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Thoracic duct

Thoracic duct  (1) begins in 
the abdomen as a dilated sac, 
the cisterna chyli, and 
passes through the aortic 
opening

It enters the thorax in the 
posterior mediastinum to 
the right of the aorta 
ascends posterior & left to the 
esophagus joins the blood 
vascular system at the left 
venous angle (3) (junction 
of the left internal jugular and 
subclavian veins)
1
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

PHRENIC NERVES

Arises from the anterior branches of 
C3-C5 nerves and lies in front of 
the anterior scalene muscle.

Runs anterior to the root of the 
lung, whereas the vagus nerve
runs posterior to the root of the 
lung.

Is accompanied by the 
pericardiophrenic vessels of the 
internal thoracic vessels descending
between the mediastinal pleura and 
the pericardium.

Innervates the fibrous pericardium, 
the mediastinal and 
diaphragmatic pleurae (sensory 
innervation), and the diaphragm
for motor and its central tendon for 
sensory.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

VAGUS NERVES

Descend from the neck in the 
thorax from the superior
through the posterior 
mediastinum where they 
form esophageal plexus

Together with the esophagus 
comes the abdominal cavity 
(T10) and forms two vagal 
trunks on the stomach

Anterior vagal trunk
terminates on the anterior 
wall of the stomach, 
posterior one along the left 
gastric artery comes to the 
celiac plexus to supply 
organs of the upper floor 
abdominal cavity
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

VAGUS NERVES
Branches in the thorax:

branches to the heart, lung, and 
esophagus

Left recurrent laryngeal nerve

approaches the aortic arch &
hooks around it lateral to the 
ligamentum arteriosum

ascends to the neck and supplies all 
the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, 
EXCEPT the cricothyroid (superior 
laryngeal nerve from cervical part 
vagus nerve supplies it)

Note: Right recurrent laryngeal
nerve arises from the right vagus at 
the root of the neck and hooks 
around the right subclavian 
artery
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Describe the structure, function and location of endothelial cells.
Describe what electron microscopy shows in an endothelial cell: pinocytotic vesicles and Weibel-Palade bodies, and the two proteins the Weibel-Palade bodies store.
Describe the structure, function and location of blood capillaries, and explain why a capillary has one incomplete tunica intima.
Relate capillary diameter to the diameter of an erythrocyte, and explain why erythrocytes pass in single file.
Describe the capillary bed, the metarteriole and the precapillary sphincter, and explain how a capillary bed is opened and closed.
Classify capillaries by leakiness — continuous, fenestrated and sinusoidal — and describe the structure, function and location of each.
Describe the structure, function and location of pericytes.
Describe the post-capillary venule, and explain margination and diapedesis of white blood cells.
Explain the clinical connections of the microcirculation: the role of pericytes in wound healing and in hemangiopericytoma, and the formation of edema when fluid builds up in the interstitial fluid (ISF).
Microcirculation Histology Lecture — Learning Outcomes

Microcirculation: Introduction
In Capillaries: No tunica media + No tunica externa 
Classification of capillaries is not possible by tunica media
Classification is based on the “leakiness” of the capillaries
In some capillaries, pericytes (“around-cells”) take the place of the tunica media and support the “lonely” endothelium
50 000 miles of capillaries

Every cell needs capillary supply

Structure:

Cells are aligned with their long axis in the directions of the blood flow (red arrow)
Flat endothelial cells with flat nuclei that protrude into the capillary lumen, because the nucleus is thicker than the surrounding thin cytoplasm. 
Tight junctions between endothelial cells 
No tunica media: no vascular smooth muscles and no vasoconstriction and no further bulging of nucleus into lumen
No tunica externa: no connective tissue
Function: 
It is the thinnest “wall” in the body: fast transport of oxygen/CO2 and nutrients/waste (exchange)
Selective blood-tissue barrier (selective: selective transport is possible, barrier: no bleeding)
Slippery smooth surface to reduce friction, prevents thrombus formation and blockage in blood flow

Inside lining of entire circulatory system (CVS + Lymphatic)

Flattened endothelial nuclei (longitudinal section); slightly protruding flat nuclei (cross section). Not round nuclei like those in arterioles.

Importance of Blood Flow Control by the Local Tissues
Local control of blood flow by tissues is important because the heart can not accommodate all the tissues needs with the adequate amount of blood.
Blood flow to tissues is kept at a level only slightly more than required to maintain full tissue oxygenation but no more than this.
By controlling local blood flow in such an exact way, tissues almost never experience oxygen and /or nutritional deficiency and the work load on the heart is kept minimal.

Causes and definition of cardiac failure
Diminished coronary blood flow (Myocardial Infarction)
Damaged heart valves
Vitamin B deficiency
Increased pressure around the heart
Primary diseases of the myocardium
			
Definition
Cardiac Failure is the inability of the heart  to pump enough blood to accommodate the needs of the body.
Speaker notes: 9

Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure
Acute effects of Moderate Cardiac Failure
:
In 
acute
 cardiac damage (Myocardial Infarction), the pumping ability of the heart is reduced resulting in:
1- Decreased cardiac output
2- Damming of blood in the veins: increased venous pressure
Speaker notes: 14

Compensated heart failure
Speaker notes: 25

Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure
Following myocardial damage, the normal cardiac output curve (Point A: cardiac output 5 L/min, atrial pressure 0 mmHg) becomes greatly lowered (
Point B
: cardiac output 2L/min, atrial pressure 4 mmHg) but does not last for long time (few seconds) because of the activation of the sympathetic system.
Speaker notes: 29

Compensation for Acute Cardiac Failure by 
Sympathetic Nervous Reflex
Acute cardiac failure activates the sympathetic nerve:
1- Baroreceptor reflex: increased sympathetic activity
2- Chemoreceptors reflex
3- Central nerve system ischemic response
4- Reflexes originating at the damaged myocardium
If the ventricular muscle is diffusely damaged, the sympathetic stimulation may strengthen this damage. 
If part of the myocardium is damaged, the normal part of cardiac musculature will contract strongly to compensate for the damaged myocardium: 
the heart will become a stronger pump
.
Speaker notes: 34

Following 
sympathetic activity
 
(maximally developed within 30sec) the new circulatory state is depicted by 
point C
 
(Cardiac output: 4.2 L/min, atrial pressure 5 mmHg).
Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure

Chronic Stage of Failure-Fluid Retention and Compensated Cardiac Output.
Following heart attack, a 
semichronic
 state begins characterized by:
1- Fluid retention by the kidneys
2- Various degrees of recovery of the heart over a period of weeks to months (Slide Nb 11)
1- 
Renal Retention of Fluid and Increase in Blood Volume Occur for Hours to Days
Urine output is lowered with decreased cardiac output (anuria for CO of 50-60%).
Moderate fluid retention in cardiac failure can be beneficial by compensating for the diminished pumping ability of the heart by:
Increasing the mean systemic filling pressure.
Distending the veins which reduces the venous resistance and facilitates blood flow to the heart.
Significant decrease in cardiac output leads to decreased blood flow through the kidney and lowering of water and salt excretion, this results in fluid retention.

Following 
water retention 
(developed within days) the new circulatory state is depicted by 
point D 
(Cardiac output: 5 L/min, atrial pressure 6 mmHg).
Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure

If the heart’s pumping capability is reduced further, 
long term fluid retention is detrimental 
because the heart is pumping at its maximal capacity and excessive fluid retention will: 
Increase the workload on the damaged heart 
Overstretch cardiac muscle
Pulmonary edema 
Extensive edema in several parts of the body: severe edema will develop in the body than can lead to death. 
How does long term fluid retention become detrimental in cardiac failure ?
Circulatory dynamics (SV and EDV) in the failing heart

(Continue slide Nb 8)
2- 
Recovery of the myocardium after myocardial infarction
After myocardial infarction, a new 
collateral blood supply 
start to penetrate the peripheral infarcted area often causing much of the muscle in the fringe to be functional again.
The viable musculature of the myocardium becomes 
hypertrophied
, thus offsetting much of the cardiac damage.
Cardiac output curve after partial recovery 
(Point D: CO 5 L/min, atrial pressure 6mmHg). The retention of fluid that has already occurred continues to maintain moderate excess of fluid. The person has essentially normal cardiovascular dynamics as long as he or she remains at rest.

Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure
Summary of the Changes that Occur After Acute Cardiac Failure- “Compensated Heart Failure”
Normal state of circulatory dynamics (point A)
State few seconds after heart attack before the activation of the sympathetic reflex (Point B)
Increased cardiac output by the sympathetic reflex (30 sec to 1 min) (Point C)
Partial recovery of Cardiac output after fluid retention (
Point D
): This final state is called 
Compensated Heart Failure

Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure
In compensated heart failure, the ability of maximal pumping of the heart is reduced to almost two and half.
The raise in atrial pressure can maintain a normal CO. Old people may have compensated heart failure without noticing it as long as they stay at rest. Any activity that requires increased pumping of the heart causes a return of the symptoms of acute heart failure. Their 
Cardiac reserve 
is reduced (refer to slide Nb.25).
Decompensated heart failure

Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure
Dynamics of Severe Cardiac Failure- “
Decompensated Heart Failure
”
In severe damaged heart, the sympathetic reflex and the fluid retention will not be able to restore a normal CO. Fluid continues to be retained and the person develops more edema which eventually leads to death: this is called
 Decompensated Heart Failure
. 
The main cause of decompensated heart failure is the incapacity of the heart to pump sufficient blood to make the kidneys excrete daily the necessary amounts of fluid.

Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure
Graphical Analysis of Decompensated Heart Failure
Point A
: Before any compensation
Point B
: CO 4L/min (
not enough for fluid excretion by kidneys
) due to sympathetic stimulation
Point C
: After one day CO 4.2 L/min
Point D
: CO did not reach 5L/min yet and atrial pressure is 9mm Hg
Point E
: More edema and fluid retention in the body and the myocardium
Point F
: increased right atrial pressure with reduced cardiac performance.
This state of heart failure is called 
Decompensated Heart Failure

Circulatory dynamics in cardiac failure
Treatment of “Decompensated Heart Failure”
Treatment involves:
1- 
Strengthening of the heart by 
cardiotonic
 drugs (Digitalis):
Digitalis inhibits the sodium-potassium pump that increase the intracellular concentration of sodium. This leads to slowing down of the sodium-calcium exchanger (usually brings sodium in and calcium out) that results in retention of calcium in the sarcoplasm for effective contraction.
2- 
Administering of 
diuretic 
to increase excretion of fluids through the kidneys
.
https://
images.app.goo.gl

Digoxin: mode of action on cardiomyocytes

Unilateral Heart failure
When the 
left ventricle 
alone fails, the mean pulmonary filling pressure increases. If the pulmonary capillary pressure rises above 28 mmHg (colloid osmotic pressure of the plasma), fluid will infiltrate from the capillaries leading to pulmonary vascular congestion and pulmonary edema. It may cause death by suffocation within 20-30 minutes following acute heart failure.
http://www.heartfailure.org/heart-failure/lungs/

Low-Output Cardiac Failure-Cardiogenic Shock
After long periods of slow progressive cardiac deterioration, the heart becomes incapable of pumping 
the minimal amount of blood required to keep the body alive
.
This is called “Cardiogenic Shock” or “Cardiac Shock”.
Vicious Circle of Cardiac Deterioration
The low arterial pressure (below 45 mmHg) leads to low pressure in the coronary artery which makes the shock progressively worse. In a heart that have a blockage in one of the major arteries, 
a fall in the coronary artery pressure below 80 mmHg can initiate the deterioration of the myocardium
. 
Normal Heart
Failing heart

Example of vicious circle of cardiac deterioration
Increased mean systemic filling pressure: 
increased preload
Vasoconstriction/stenosis:
 
increased afterload

Low-Output Cardiac Failure-Cardiogenic Shock
Physiological treatment of Vicious Circle of Cardiac Deterioration
Immediate administration of digitalis
Infusion of whole blood, plasma, or a blood-pressure raising drug.
Surgical removing of the clot in the coronary arteries
Catheterizing the blocked coronary artery and infusion of 
streptokinase
 or 
tissue-type plasminogen activator
 enzyme to dissolve the clot.

Edema in Patients with Cardiac Failure
Acute Cardiac Failure 
does not cause immediate 
Peripheral
 Edema
Right or left heart failure is very slow to cause Peripheral edema because:
Aortic pressure falls (from 100 mmHg to 13mmHg)
Right atrial pressure rises (0 mmHg to 13 mmHg)
Capillary pressure falls (17 mm Hg to 13 mm Hg)
Therefore, severe acute cardiac failure 
causes a fall in peripheral capillary 
pressure rather than a rise: 
No peripheral edema
.

Long-Term Fluid Retention by the Kidneys- the Cause of Peripheral Edema in Persisting Heart Failure
Causes of reduced renal output of urine during cardiac failure.
1- Decreased glomerular filtration rate due to
:
Reduced arterial pressure
Intense sympathetic vasoconstriction of the afferent arterioles of the kidneys
2- Activation of the renin-angiotensin system and increased reabsorption of water and salt by the renal tubules
Reduced blood flow to the kidneys initiates the secretion of renin which promotes the secretion of angiotensin II. 
AngII
 constricts the renal arterioles thus reducing the blood flow through the kidneys and promoting reabsorption of salts and water from the tubules. 
AngII
 also acts on the epithelial tubular cells to promote reabsorption of water and salts.
3- Increased Aldosterone secretion
AngII
 stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone. Also, increased extracellular Potassium stimulates aldosterone secretion.
Aldosterone promotes absorption of sodium which eventually results in absorption of water (osmotic pressure). Reabsorbed sodium and other anions promote the secretion of ADH resulting in further retention of water by the kidneys.
4- Activation of the sympathetic system
Constriction of renal afferent arterioles
Reabsorption for water and salts (Alpha-adrenergic receptors on tubular epithelial cells)
Stimulation of RAS
Stimulation of ADH
Edema in Patients with Cardiac Failure

Role of the Atrial Natriuretic Peptide to Delay the Onset of Cardiac Decompensation
Stretch of the atrial wall results in the secretion of ANP. Increased atrial pressure during heart failure leads to the release of ANP that acts on the kidney to stimulate the secretion of water and salt (
Natural protector of extreme symptoms in decompensated heart failure
).
Edema in Patients with Cardiac Failure

Acute Pulmonary Edema in Late-stage Heart Failure- Another Vicious Circle
Vicious circle leading to acute pulmonary edema
:
1- Damming of blood into the lungs
2- Pulmonary edema
3- Diminished degree of oxygenation of blood
4- Further weakening of the cardiac muscle due to low levels of oxygen which causes vasodilation of the arterioles
5- Increased venous return
6- Accentuation of the previous steps leading to Death.
Therapy 
:
1- Tourniquets on arms and legs (sequester blood in veins, decrease workload on the left side of the heart)
2- Rapidly acting diuretic
3- Pure oxygen
4- Rapidly acting 
Cardiotonic
 drug
Edema in Patients with Cardiac Failure
What is cardiac reserve?

Cardiac reserve is the maximum percentage that the cardiac output can increase above normal. The graph below shows different cardiac reserve that are in association with cardiac conditions.
Diagnosis of Low Cardiac Reserve- Exercise Test
.
1- Immediate and extreme shortness of breath
2- Extreme muscle fatigue 
3- Excessive increase in heart rate
Cardiac Reserve

Graphical Analysis of Decompensated Heart Failure

Treatment of Decompensated Heart Disease with Digitalis
Digitalis is given to strengthen the heart. The final steady state condition of the circulation is defined by the crossing point of the three curves: the cardiac output curve, the venous return curve, and the critical level for normal fluid balance. At this point, the 
decompensation of the heart failure has been compensated
.

Graphical Analysis 
of High-Output Cardiac Failure
Arteriovenous fistula
: 
Large opening between a large artery and a large vein leading to decreased total vascular peripheral resistance. If the person tries to exercise, he or she will have a low cardiac reserve because of increased cardiac output near to maximal range. The situation will resemble a cardiac failure and is called “High Output Failure”.
Beriberi
Avitaminosis leads to weakened heart that decreases the blood flow to the kidney resulting in fluid retention (increase mean systemic filling pressure).
